**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 96, verses 6–19:**

«﴿Nay! Indeed, man does transgress﴾. It was revealed some time later concerning Abu Jahl, who was hostile to the Messenger of Allah and forbade him from praying in the Mosque. It is related that he said: "If I see Muhammad prostrating at the Ka'bah, I will surely step on his neck." It is further related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rebuked him, scolded him, and threatened him. Abu Jahl said: "Does Muhammad threaten me? By Allah, no one in the valley has a greater assembly than mine!" It is also reported that he intended to prevent him from praying, but then he refrained. ("Nay!") is a rebuke to the one who disbelieved in the blessing of Allah upon him through his transgression, even though no antecedent has been mentioned, because the context points to it. ﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾, that is, he exceeds the limit. ﴿When he sees himself self-sufficient﴾. The agent (fa'il) is the pronoun of "man," and the object pronoun also refers to him. "Ra'a" here is from the seeing of the heart. Both pronouns may refer to the same person when they are attached, as when you say: "ra'aytunī ṣadīqaka" (I saw myself as your friend). This is not possible with other verbs, so one does not say "Zayd ḍarabahu" (Zayd struck him) when both pronouns refer to Zayd.

The majority of readers (qurra') read (أنْ رَآهُ) with an alif after the hamza, and this alif is the lam of the verb. It has been said that some transmitted a reading without the alif, and this is the narration of Ibn Mujahid from him. He said: "It is an error and not permissible," but one should not call him erroneous; rather one should seek a justification for it. The alif has indeed been dropped in similar forms. He (the poet) said:

"Al-'Ajjāj advised me in what he advised me,"

meaning "wa-ṣānī" (he advised me), dropping the alif, which is the lam of the verb. It has also been dropped in the present tense of "ra'ā" in their saying: "aṣāba al-nāsa juhdun wa-law tara ahla Makkah" (hardship befell the people, and if you could see the people of Makkah...). This is a dropping that is not regular (lā yanqās), but when the transmission of it is sound it must be accepted. The recitations came according to the language of the Arabs, both the regular (qiyās) and the anomalous (shādhdh).

﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾, that is, the return (al-ruj'ā), a verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern fu'lā; the alif in it is the feminine marker. In this is a threat to the transgressor who thinks himself self-sufficient, and a belittling of what he is in, since his end is the Resurrection, the Reckoning and the Recompense for his transgression.

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾, ﴿a servant when he prays﴾. It has preceded that he is Abu Jahl. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "None of the exegetes differed that the one who forbids is Abu Jahl, and that the servant who prays is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." End of quote. In al-Kashshaf: "al-Hasan said: he is Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who used to forbid Salman from praying." Al-Tabrizi said: "What is meant by the prayer here is the Dhuhr prayer. It has been said: it was the first congregation established in Islam. Abu Bakr, 'Ali and a group of the foremost (sābiqūn) were with him. Abu Talib passed by him with his son Ja'far, and said to him: 'Join the wing of your cousin's son,' and he went away rejoicing. Abu Talib then began to say:

"Indeed 'Ali and Ja'far are my trust in the time of calamity and distress,
By Allah, I will not abandon the Prophet, nor will one abandon him who is of my lineage,
Do not abandon him, and help your cousin, my brother from my mother and my father among them."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoiced at this. The address in (أرَأيْتَ) is apparently to the Messenger, and likewise the second (أرَأيْتَ), and the coherence of the pronouns is what the structure requires. It has also been said that (أرَأيْتَ) is addressed to the disbeliever: he turned to the disbeliever and said: "Have you seen, O disbeliever, if his prayer is guidance, a call to Allah, and a command to piety, would you forbid him in spite of that?" The pronoun in (إنْ كانَ) and in (إنْ كَذَّبَ) refers to the one who forbids. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: inform me about the one who forbids some of the servants of Allah from their prayer, if that forbidder is upon a sound way in what he forbids of worshipping Allah, and was commanding righteousness and piety in what he commands of idol-worship, as he believes; and likewise if he was upon denial of the truth and turning away from the true religion, as we say."

﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾, and observes his conditions, whether his guidance or his error, and will recompense him according to that. This is a threat. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The pronoun in ﴿if he is upon guidance﴾ refers to the one who prays. This was said by al-Farra' and others. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays﴾, while he is upon guidance and commands piety, and the forbidder is a denier who turns away from the Reminder. That is: how strange is this! Does Abu Jahl not know that Allah the Exalted sees him and knows his deed? This is a confirmation and a rebuke." End of quote. He said: "Whoever makes the pronoun in (إنْ كانَ) refer to the one who prays, he adds to the act of prayer the command to piety, because Abu Jahl was distressed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that prayer and calling to Allah the Exalted were both ordered, and because he was only found in two matters: reforming himself by performing the prayer, and reforming others by commanding piety." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ completes the rebuke and the threat according to the three conditions (al-tawfiqāt al-thalāthah), each of which suits the others; they are brought in a sequence, then the sufficient threat is given covering all of them briefly and concisely, and with each statement there is an implied complement in which the expressions can extend, and ''Does he not know'' indicates it and suffices."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: what is the object of (أرَأيْتَ)? I say: (the one who forbids) together with the conditional clause, and they are in the position of the two objects. If you say: where is the answer of the condition? I say: it is omitted, its estimate being: ﴿if he is upon guidance or commands piety﴾, ﴿does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ It was omitted because its mention in the answer of the second condition indicates it. If you say: how is it correct that (ألَمْ يَعْلَمْ) should be an answer to the condition? I say: just as it is correct in your saying: 'If I honour you, will you honour me?' and 'If Zayd does good to you, will you do good to him?' If you say: what is the second (أرَأيْتَ) and its placement between the two objects of (أرَأيْتَ)? I say: it is superfluous, repeated for emphasis." End of quote.

We have discussed the rules of (أرَأيْتَ) in the sense of "inform me" in several places, among them in Surah al-An'am, and we have elaborated on them in the commentary on al-Tashil. What al-Zamakhshari established here does not run according to what we established. Among that: he claimed that the conditional clause is in the position of a single object, and the relative pronoun is the other. According to us, the second object can only be an interrogative clause, like His saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away and gave a little and then held back?﴾ [al-Najm: 33–34] ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen?﴾ [al-Najm: 35], ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said: "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ [Maryam: 77] ﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾ [Maryam: 78], ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58] ﴿Is it you who create it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59], and it is frequent in the Qur'an. So this verse is to be parsed according to that rule, and the relative pronoun (الذي) is made the object of the first (أرَأيْتَ). Then comes (أرَأيْتَ), which requires two objects, and the second and third (أرَأيْتَ) are likewise; the object of the second and third (أرَأيْتَ) is omitted and refers to (الذي يَنْهى) in them, or to (عَبْدًا) in the second, and to (الذي يَنْهى) in the third, according to the earlier difference over the return of the pronoun. The interrogative clause is claimed by three seekers (ṭawālib), so we say: the second object of the first (أرَأيْتَ) is omitted, namely the interrogative clause, indicated by the later interrogative, because it indicates it. The object of the last (أرَأيْتَ) is omitted, because the object of the first (أرَأيْتَ) indicates it. Both were omitted for the second (أرَأيْتَ), because the first indicates its first object, and the other indicates for the third (أرَأيْتَ) its other object. These seekers do not seek it by way of contention (tanāzu'), because clauses cannot validly be supplied as pronouns; rather this is from the category of omission outside of contention. As for al-Zamakhshari's permitting an interrogative clause to occur as the answer of a condition without a fa' (فاء), I know of no one who permitted it. Rather they stated the obligation of the fa' in everything that demands a request in some way, and it is not permissible to omit it except in poetic necessity.

The agent (fa'il) is the pronoun of "man," and the object pronoun also refers to him. "Ra'a" here is from the seeing of the heart. Both pronouns may refer to the same person when they are attached, as when you say: "ra'aytunī ṣadīqaka" (I saw myself as your friend). This is not possible with other verbs, so one does not say "Zayd ḍarabahu" (Zayd struck him) when both pronouns refer to Zayd.

The majority of readers (qurra') read (أنْ رَآهُ) with an alif after the hamza, and this alif is the lam of the verb. It has been said that some transmitted a reading without the alif, and this is the narration of Ibn Mujahid from him. He said: "It is an error and not permissible," but one should not call him erroneous; rather one should seek a justification for it. The alif has indeed been dropped in similar forms. "Al-'Ajjāj advised me in what he advised me,"

meaning "wa-ṣānī" (he advised me), dropping the alif, which is the lam of the verb. This is a dropping that is not regular (lā yanqās), but when the transmission of it is sound it must be accepted. "Indeed 'Ali and Ja'far are my trust in the time of calamity and distress,
